Items.Authors: Ariadna Calcines Rosario, Sarah Matthews, Hamish Reid
Items.Title: Developments on slicers in the EUV for the first EUV integral field spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The image slicer technology is widely applied in the IR, Visible and, more recently, UV spectral ranges. We present the latest developments of this technology for their first application in the Extreme Ultra-Violet (EUV) regime at 18 nm. The main challenges relate to: surface roughness, which we have reduced from 1 to 0.2 nm RMS; the novel developments on Multi-layer (M-L) dielectric coatings for two simultaneous spectral windows centred at 18 and 25 nm and the first application to slicers; and the slicer width, for which we have manufactured the thinnest slicers in the world with a width of 15 microns. The activities undertaken to increase TRL and the next steps towards achieving the space qualification will be presented. These developments are proposed for the first EUV integral field spectrograph, SISA (Spectral Imager of the Solar Atmosphere), included in the SPARK solar mission proposal selected by ESA in Step 1 for an M-class mission opportunity.

Items.Authors: Melanie Ulitschka, Enrico Hilpert, Tatjana Porwol, Luxuan Cai, Ralf Steinkopf, Sandra Müller, Mathias Rohde, Markus Unger, Robert Jende, Peter Weide, Jan Kinast, Stefan Risse
Items.Title: Direct ultra-precise processing of optical freeform RSA6061 surfaces with shape correction and smoothing techniques
Items.Abstract: Technical aluminium alloys like RSA6061 are essential for high-performance mirror devices. The surface error topography after common ultra-precise machining meet the requirements for infrared applications. However, for shorter wavelengths such as VIS or EUV, optical surface quality demands are much higher. Usually, a nickel-phosphorous (NiP) coating is needed due to the challenges of ultra-precision machining of aluminium, which often results in significant surface roughening. A promising solution for direct aluminium machining combines ion beam figuring (IBF) with chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) to effectively reduce both form errors and roughness.

Items.Authors: Ondrej Kitzler, Christian Schwab, Julian Stürmer, Jacob Pember, Dane Zielinski-Nicolson, Thorsten Fuehrer, Jonathan Crass, Gert Raskin, David Coutts
Items.Title: Doppler-free spectroscopy of the Cesium D1 line as absolute wavelength reference for the iLocater near-IR Etalon calibrator
Items.Abstract: Stabilised broadband etalons are ideal calibrators for extreme-precision radial-velocity spectrometers. Due to inherent drift, they must be referenced to an absolute frequency standard, such as an atomic absorption line. We have expanded our etalon-locking technique using saturated absorption spectroscopy of alkali atoms to the Cs D1 line at 895 nm. This wavelength lies just outside the iLocater spectral range but remains within the single-mode range of the fibers used here. Locking the etalon close to, but outside, the spectrometer bandpass avoids suppressing the atomic-probe laser and prevents its light from entering the instrument. We have built a custom ECDL at this wavelength, producing narrow-linewidth, tunable laser light. Additional saturated-absorption lines also allow probing etalon stability at multiple wavelengths; currently available in our lab are 780 nm (Rb D2), 852 nm (Cs D2), and 895 nm (Cs D1).

Items.Authors: Xana Delpueyo, Juan Francisco Hernández Cabrera
Items.Title: DRAGO Project: SWIR cameras for nano- and micro-satellites
Items.Abstract: IACTEC-Space is an IAC initiative for developing advanced instrumentation for small satellites dedicated to astronomy and Earth observation. One of its goal is to monitor Earth’s dynamic processes from orbit with compact, high-performance imaging systems. The first instruments, DRAGO-1 and DRAGO-2, operate in the SWIR range (1.1 µm and 1.6 µm) using an uncooled InGaAs detector based on proprietary design, unique in the market. Launched in 2021 and 2023, respectively, they enabled imaging of the 2021 La Palma eruption and the 2023 Tenerife wildfire. DRAGO-1 provides 300 m resolution, while DRAGO-2 reaches 50 m, improvable to 30 m via non-interpolated super-resolution. An upgraded DRAGO-2 is onboard ALISIO-1, the first Canarian satellite. Current developments include IACSAT ASTRO-1 and DRAGO-3, featuring four NIR/SWIR bands with ~10 m/pixel resolution, enhancing natural disaster detection within the future Canarian Earth-observation constellation.

Items.Authors: Mona El Morsy, Olivier Guyon, Barnaby Norris, Sergio Leon-Saval, Sébastien Vievard, Julien Lozi, Thayne Currie, Yoo Jung Kim, Mike Fitzgerald, Nemanja Jovanovic
Items.Title: Efficient, simultaneous exoplanet spectroscopy, wavefront control and calibration at deep contrast with hybrid mode-selective photonic lanterns
Items.Abstract: HWO aims to directly image objects orbiting Sun-like stars using a 6m telescope capable of high-contrast imaging (10^-10) and spectroscopy to search for biosignatures in habitable-zone planets. Lab and ground-based telescope projects show SMFs effectiveness to enhance spectral stability and reduce modal noise, enabling SMF-fed spectrographs in future space missions like HWO. Long integrations require precise wavefront measurement for deep contrast and robust starlight calibration. Photonic lanterns (PLs) couple light over a broader angular range, converting a multimode input into multiple single-mode outputs. At the focal plane, they act as compact wavefront sensors. The Hybrid-Mode Selective PL (HMSPL) directs planet light into a central SMF for mid-R spectroscopy while adjacent SMFs route speckle light to a low-R spectrograph, eliminating NCPA and optimizing throughput. We present HMSPL’s dual role and planned tests at UTSA's high contrast imaging lab and at SCExAO/Subaru Telescope

Items.Authors: Marco Colussi, Marco Mattietto, Leo Colussi, Gianmarco Franceschini, Andrea Fadalti, Nicola Casoni, Pascal Martinez, Mark Wallace
Items.Title: ELT Dome project: from final design to first rotation on site
Items.Abstract: The ELT Dome, now in advanced construction and early commissioning at Cerro Armazones, combines a 90-m concrete pier with an 80-m-high rotating steel enclosure weighing about 6000 t. The hemispherical structure, equipped with slit doors providing a 42-m aperture, has completed major assembly steps and full rotation tests on its 36 trolleys. Thermal control is ensured through fire-resistant cladding, a dedicated windscreen and 89 louvers, and a custom HVAC system stabilizing the 300000 m³ chamber. The paper presents the final design and key construction and early commissioning results.

Items.Authors: Nour Skaf, Olivier Guyon, Sebastien Vievard, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Manon Le Teuff
Items.Title: Enabling photonic lantern high contrast imaging with DrWHO
Items.Abstract: We present a new photonic pathway toward high-contrast imaging by applying the DrWHO empirical optimization framework to a photonic lantern. Classical DrWHO implementations rely on separate science and wavefront sensors, limiting performance from several issues. Replacing the focal-plane detector with a photonic lantern feeding a single detector provides simultaneous spectral and spatial information, enabling high contrast at ~0.5l/D angular separations. In this architecture, single-mode fibers act as directional spatial filters: concentrating stellar light into one fiber makes the remaining fibers sensitive to off-axis planetary signals. DrWHO iteratively learns the WFS state that maximizes a chosen metric, either for blind searches - by driving stellar light into one fiber - or targeted detection, by optimizing the coupling of stellar and planetary flux across selected fibers. Items.Authors: Stefan Seifried, Sebastian Stahringer, Sebastian Stoebenau
Items.Title: Enabling the next generation of space optics: ultra-precision manufacturing for large-diameter mirrors
Items.Abstract: Advanced optical components are essential in many high-tech applications, ranging from simple aspheres to complex freeform surfaces and from microlenses to large space optics. Their production involves multiple grinding steps to form the geometry, followed by polishing to achieve optical quality and correct shape and mid-spatial-frequency errors. OptoTech, part of the Schunk Group, offers a complete portfolio for precision-optics manufacturing, including tooling, fixtures, advanced grinding and polishing machines, and production monitoring systems. Recent developments include the UPG 500 CNC and UPG 1000 CNC machining centers for large-scale optics, delivering high shape accuracy and minimal sub-surface damage. Combined with OptoTech’s advanced polishing processes, these technologies reduce production time and ensure a fast return on investment.

Items.Authors: Elvio Hernández Suárez, Dylan Carroll, Haroldo Lorenzo Hernández, Iñigo Arizaga, Enrique Joven, Javier De Miguel-Hernández
Items.Title: Engineering Challenges in the Integration of the DALI Cryogenic Dark-Matter Prototype
Items.Abstract: The Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC) is developing the DALI (Dark-photons & Axion-Like particles Interferometer) prototype, an astro-particle instrument aimed at detecting axions and paraphotons in the 6–60 GHz range. The system integrates a permanent-magnet yoke generating a ~0.65 T magnetic field, a cryostat, and a high-frequency detection chain within a compact and mechanically demanding environment. This paper provides an overview of the main subsystems and their mechanical implementation.  The work focuses on the integration challenges related to the assembly of the permanent magnets, operation under strong magnetic fields, and the cool-down of a large thermal mass to cryogenic temperatures. Results from initial thermal cycling tests are presented, including mechanical stability and system behaviour under combined magnetic, vacuum, and cryogenic conditions.

Items.Authors: Douglas Miller, Greg Taylor, Jennifer Power, Sam Ragland
Items.Title: Enhanced seeing mode at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory: a comparison with ground layer AO
Items.Abstract: The SOUL Adaptive Optics System at the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory (LBTO), in conjunction with the f/30 camera on the LUCI (LBT Utility Camera in the Infrared) instruments, delivers diffraction-limited image quality with a 30”x30” field of view. The AO system includes a low-mode form delivering only 10 modes of correction (tip, tilt, focus, 2 × astigmatism, 2 × coma, 2 × trefoil and spherical) to remove jitter and residual aberrations. This low-mode form of operation is referred to as Enhanced Seeing mode (ESM) and is found to consistently provide significant angular resolution across the full 4’x4’ field of view of the wide field f/N3.75 camera on the LUCI instruments. In this paper we will show the results of simulations which will compare ESM to Ground Layer AO (GLAO). We will also compare ESM data with engineering data taken with the ARGOS GLAO system. We intend to demonstrate the superb quality of ESM observations at the LBTO.

Items.Authors: Thomas Procter, Glenn Walters, Nicholas Law, Alex Bucheli, Jonathan Carney, Hank Corbett, James Dockery, Megan Dubay, Shannon Fitton, Lawrence Machia, William Marshall, Michael Ronco, Donovan Schlekat, Alan Vasquez Soto
Items.Title: Environmental isolation for the Argus Array: comparative analysis of air curtains and glass windows
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array utilizes a unique pseudo-focal design to allow multiple optical tube assemblies to observe through a single, shared oculus. This configuration allows the telescope enclosure to be sealed for enhanced stability. Using Python and scripted-simulations in Zemax OpticStudio, we analyze oculus sizing and vignetting limits for the Array. Furthermore, we compare the viability of a large fused silica window against an air curtain system, centering our findings around vignetting, ghosting, transmission, point spread function performance, and the collective effect on limiting magnitude.

Items.Authors: Erica E. Lugo-Ibarra, Laurence Sabin, Yair Krongold, Wen-Ping Chen, David Hiriart Garcia, Liliana Figueroa Carrillo, Alfonso H. Franco, Joel V. Herrera-Vazquez, Eduardo Lopez Angeles, Francisco Javier Valenzuela Vargas, Gerardo Sierra Díaz, Fernando Quiros, Yi Chou, Chow-Choong Ngeow, Yen-Chen Pan, Ting-Wan Chen, Ming-Hsin Chang, Anli Tsai, Yung-Hsin Chang, Lung-Ting Wang, Julio Ramirez, Jesús González
Items.Title: Environmental site characterization for the remote operation of the TransPacific 2m Telescope (TP2m) at San Pedro Mártir National Park, Mexico
Items.Abstract: This presentation describes the environmental site characterization conducted for the TransPacific 2m Telescope (TP2m), a collaborative project between UNAM (Mexico) and the National Central University (Taiwan) at San Pedro Mártir National Park, a world-class astronomical site. The talk outlines the key characteristics that guided the site definition and the strategies implemented to minimize environmental impact, considering national environmental and regulatory criteria. Results confirm that the selected site meets all requirements for sustainable telescope operation, establishing a replicable model for the integration of environmental planning and astronomical development in protected natural areas

Items.Authors: Jessica S. Li, Aiden Shaheen, Keri Hoadley, Greyson Davis, Fernando Cruz Aguirre
Items.Title: Establishing a foundation for far-UV spectropolarimetry
Items.Abstract: This work presents the design and initial validation of a reflective element polarizer (REP) for future far-ultraviolet (FUV) astrophysical instrumentation. Polarimetry provides unique diagnostics of dust alignment, magnetic fields, and potential biosignature-related scattering, yet traditional transmissive polarizers have low throughput in the UV. A 3-mirror REP configuration is evaluated through Zemax (ZOS-API) simulations to quantify polarization-dependent throughput as a function of wavelength, coating, and incidence angle. Complementary benchtop measurements at 405, 520, and 639 nm provide early experimental verification of polarization behavior. This proof-of-concept establishes a pathway toward efficient reflective polarizers that could enable next-generation FUV instrumentation for studies of dust, star and planet formation, and UV-sensitive biosignatures.

Items.Authors: Savitha M. S., Nagaraju K., Raveena Khan, Mohammed H. Modi, P. K. Yadav, R. K. Gupta
Items.Title: EUV polarimeter optics based on metal coatings
Items.Abstract: Direct measurement of the solar coronal magnetic field is key to understanding heating and other processes in the solar corona. The Hanle effect in EUV spectral lines offers a promising diagnostic for probing the coronal vector magnetic field, but requires precise polarization measurements; yet, no EUV spectropolarimeter currently exists for such observation.  Reflective polarizers near Brewster’s angle offer a promising approach for an EUV polarimeter. This study evaluates suitable mirror coatings for an EUV polarimeter operating in the 500–1000 Å band. Zemax simulations identify platinum and iridium as promising candidates for a polarimeter mirror. To experimentally validate these results, platinum-coated samples were characterized at the soft X-ray reflectivity beamline (BL-4) of the INDUS-1 synchrotron at RRCAT. The measured Rs/Rp ratios confirm strong polarization power and show good agreement with theoretical predictions.

Items.Authors: Faustine Cantalloube, Olivier Absil, Valentin Christiaens, Marc Van Droogenbroeck, Carles Cantero Mitjans, Anthony Cioppa, Antoine Alaguero, Briley Lewis, Claudia Toci, Félix Sauvourel, Iain Hammond, Johan Mazoyer, Markus Bonse, Nitya Pandey, Matthias Samland, Sebastien Pierard, Sandrine Juillard
Items.Title: Exoplanet imaging data challenge phase 3: imaging circumplanetary disks
Items.Abstract: Advanced high-contrast image processing techniques are an essential ingredient making it possible to unveil faint circumstellar signals. Launched in 2019, the Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge is a community-wide effort that offers a platform to fairly compare the latest algorithms developed over the past 20 years. After a first phase focused on the detection of point sources (exoplanets), then a second phase focused on the characterization of point sources (astrometry and spectro-photometry), the working group is preparing a third phase focused on extended source imaging. In this third phase, we will provide the community with a curated ensemble of high-contrast data set in which we injected synthetic circumstellar disks, as well as forming planets within. The morphologies and flux distributions of the injected synthetic disks are representative of the diversity of observed disks thus far thanks to high-contrast imaging instruments.

Items.Authors: J.Ph. Amans
Items.Title: EXORCIST: suppression of fibre-interface back-reflections in astronomical spectrographs
Items.Abstract: We present EXORCIST, a simple and practical solution that is compatible with standard fibre mounting and polishing processes and which significantly reduces back-reflections at the fibre interface. The approach enables substantial suppression of ghost images while preserving mechanical robustness and manufacturability. This solution is particularly relevant for fibre-fed spectrographs requiring high contrast and low stray-light performance.  EXORCIST : the ghost image killer !

Items.Authors: Sylvestre Lacour, Mathias Nowak, Oscar Carrión-González, Johan Kosmalski, Jason Spyromilio, Célia Desgrange, Elsa Huby
Items.Title: Expanding the VLTI
Items.Abstract: With the VLTI, ESO already possesses a unique observational parameter space for discoveries: unmatched angular resolution, astrometry, and contrast range. Can we build on this infrastructure to make it an imager? In this talk, we will assess the scientific opportunities that would arise from expanding the VLTI facility with four additional 8-meter telescopes and baseline lengths of up to 220 m — enabling, for example, imaging of Galactic objects at sub-AU scales and extragalactic objects at parsec scales. Although the cost issue is not on the table right now, it will inevitably arise at some point. We will therefore address a crucial aspect of the problem: proposing a simple way to expand the VLTI observatory and to build inexpensive, fast, 8-meter telescopes. This dual approach — combining high-stakes science with a project that builds on existing infrastructure — could be the best path for optical interferometry in the 2040s decade.

Items.Authors: Bogdan Vasilescu, Pierre Piron, Fabien Schmutz, Eugenio Di Iorio, Ralph Snel, Jérôme Loïcq
Items.Title: Experimental validation of a versatile method for snapshot full Stokes spectropolarimetry
Items.Abstract: The capacity to measure the polarization state of light is crucial for fields ranging from astronomy to biomedical imaging. However, a significant gap exists in instrumentation for compact, robust spectropolarimeters that can perform complete, snapshot measurements across a broad waveband. It is a gap that primarily affects sectors operating in harsh environments, such as the space sector. To address this, we developed a novel spectropolarimeter architecture centred on a set of three birefringent prisms. This core component enables high-fidelity, hyperspectral polarization imaging in a single shot. Experimental validation of a laboratory demonstrator confirms the technology's viability, with performance characterization at multiple wavelengths demonstrating accurate polarization recovery. This presentation outlines the instrument's operational principles, calibration methodology, and demodulation processes, laying the foundation for future miniaturized polarimetric systems.

Items.Authors: Prasanna G. Deshmukh, Gracia G, Phanindra D. V. S., Tsewang Stanzin, Sonam Jorphail, Tashi Tsering Mahay, Tsewang Gyalson, Tsewang Dorjai, Amit Kumar, Dorje Angchuk, Ramya M. Anche
Items.Title: Experimental vibration analysis of the 2-m Himalayan Chandra Telescope for control system development
Items.Abstract: In this paper, we present results from a dedicated vibration measurement campaign on the 2-m Himalayan Chandra Telescope conducted in August 2025 using high-sensitivity accelerometers and a custom-built, high-speed data logger. The accelerometer sensors were installed at structurally significant places on the telescope to capture broadband and transient disturbances caused by the structure, axis motion, wind loading, and other subsystems. By high-rate measurements, we were able to extract the vibration spectra, modal characteristics, coherence between structural components, and temporal evolution under tracking and slewing, which directly impact pointing stability and wave-front quality. The findings provide an essential input for optimising the HCT control system architecture and improving the vibration rejection performance. The experiment has also validated the importance of incorporating these vibration sensors as a monitoring and diagnostics system with the HCT control system.

Items.Authors: Joseph W. Barrow, Jon S. Lawrence, Aaron Omadutt, Roelof S. de Jong
Items.Title: Exploration of small footprint stick-slip piezoelectric actuators for use in the FLEX fibre positioner system for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST)
Items.Abstract: This work presents a novel stick-slip piezoelectric actuator for the FLEX fibre positioner, addressing the challenge of reducing footprint while maintaining precision in next-generation multi-object spectroscopic instruments such as the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST). The actuator combines compact geometry (3.2 mm diameter, 70 mm length) with high-resolution incremental motion, low power consumption, and high reliability. Three actuators can be integrated into a 6.2 mm diameter circle, enabling a simplified, single-plane assembly. This design offers a promising solution for miniaturized, accurate fibre positioning in wide-field spectroscopic applications.

Items.Authors: Younes Chahid, Tassos Aretos, Will Cochrane, Katherine Morris, David Isherwood, Zeshan Ali, Graham Wilks, Noah Schwartz, Anmol Goyal, Marcell Westsik, Alastair Macleod, Steve Watson, David Lunney, Bradley Frank
Items.Title: Exploring generative design AI tools for astronomical instrumentation: a CubeSat chassis case study
Items.Abstract: Generative design artificial intelligence (AI) tools are currently used in multiple scientific fields, yet their adoption in mechanical engineering computer-aided design (CAD) remains limited due to a lack of disseminated case studies, limited availability of accessible tools, insufficient training in CAD data, and the absence of universal editable file formats.     Mechanical design for astronomical instrumentation faces increasing complexity in thermal, vibrational, and mechanical requirements alongside tight project deadlines. This paper presents a practical evaluation of Autodesk Fusion generative design capabilities applied to chassis design for the A-DOT CubeSat mission. Our analysis establishes clear criteria for determining when generative design tools become advantageous over traditional CAD approaches, considering component criticality, available manufacturing methods, design complexity, and part constraints.

Items.Authors: Theodore A. Grosson, Deborah M. Lokhorst, Alan W. McConnachie
Items.Title: Exploring the trade-space of distributed aperture telescopes in spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Scientific programs targeting the faintest objects push modern telescopes to increasingly large sizes, high costs and high design complexities. For observations in which high angular resolution is not necessary, an innovative, cheaper strategy to a large diameter telescope is to use many small telescopes in place of a single large aperture, as demonstrated by instruments such as the Dragonfly Telephoto Array, the Huntsman Telescope, and the Condor Array Telescope. In this work, we discuss the merits of so-called "distributed aperture telescopes," considering especially the use case of spectroscopic observations of low surface brightness galaxies. We compare the cost and simulated scientific performance of different configurations of apertures, detectors, and other components, minimizing cost while maximizing performance. Finally, we describe a concept of this type of telescope that would be able to observe spectra of faint galaxies at a lower cost than major facilities.

Items.Authors: Manuel A. Quijada, Javier G. Del Hoyo, Luis V. Rodriguez de Marcos, Breann N. Sitarski, Edward J. Wollack, Andrew W. Howe, David R. Boris, Scott G. Walton, Mateo Batkis, John J. Hennessy
Items.Title: Exposure of highly reflective Far-Ultraviolet Coatings to LEO environment for TRL advancement for the Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: Recent developments in performing aluminum (Al) coatings protected with different F-based overcoats offer unprecedented reflectance performance in the FUV in addition to improved environmental stability. These new coating technologies result from collaborations between the Goddard Space Flight Center and two other institutions (NRL and JPL). In this paper, we report on environmental/material property characterization of several of these new Al-based FUV coatings before and after they were flown for 6 months in the International Space Station during the Materials International Space Station Experiment-20th experiment (MISSE-20) to advance the TRL for these mirror coating technologies.

Items.Authors: James P. Hamilton, Nicholas J. Baker, Noah R. Milder
Items.Title: Extended lifetime astronomical metal mirror coatings: maintain reflectivity and 100x reduction in pinholes using polymer cleaning before metal coating
Items.Abstract: Pinholes in metallic mirror coatings increase scatter, permit unwanted transmission, and act as initiation sites for under-film corrosion and adhesion loss. Pinhole formation is strongly influenced by substrate and chamber cleanliness and by particulate spatter during deposition. Here we present measurements from a precision pinhole-quantification instrument developed to characterize sputtered and PVD-deposited metal mirrors. Applying an Apply-Dry-Peel First Contact polymer treatment to substrates prior to deposition produced a dramatic reduction in pinhole density and a marked increase in film adhesion. Across multiple metals (Al, Au, Cr, Ag), aluminum showed the largest improvement, with pinhole counts reduced by nearly two orders of magnitude relative to untreated controls; in some treated samples, pinholes were not detected within our measurement limits. The combination of improved adhesion and reduced defect-site density suggests a path to more robust aluminum mirror coatings.

Items.Authors: Ana Iglesias Moreno, Paloma López Reyes, Alejandro García Cañas, Carlos Honrado Benítez, Nuria Gutierrez Luna, Francesc Valls Vicent, María Frutos Pastor, Ana Inés Gómez de Castro, Juan Ignacio Larruquert
Items.Title: Extra-narrowband mirrors for the vacuum ultraviolet: robustness and performance under simulated space conditions
Items.Abstract: Far UV band-pass filters have been identified by NASA as a high-priority technological gap. Conventional narrowband reflective filters typically achieve bandwidths of ~20 nm. Yet, narrower FUV filters are demanded for future observatories requiring the detection of specific spectral lines, such as the Observatorio Ultravioleta Lunar (OUL/UCM).  Ultra-narrowband filters with ~4 nm bandwidth (FWHM), peak reflectance >70%, tunable in the 120-200-nm range have been recently developed at GOLD-FOTION. They consist in AlF₃/MgF₂ multilayer coatings. We’ll present these filters along with their increased maturation level (TRL) for space instrumentation. The filters were tested for thermal cycling, gamma radiation, and humidity. The filters remained mostly unaffected by these tests. This demonstrates their robustness, that points to a TRL 5 towards their use in space environments. This supports their potential for next-generation FUV observatories such as OUL.

Items.Authors: David Schiminovich
Items.Title: Extremely wide-field, multi-object, high-resolution spectrograph designs for future large aperture, diffraction-limited far- and near-ultraviolet space missions
Items.Abstract: A key systems-engineering challenge for future large-aperture UV space telescopes is enabling high-resolution UV spectroscopy of sparse targets distributed across wide fields. Current Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) concepts employ IFU microshutters or slicers with fields of regard of only a few arcminutes or tens of arcseconds, limiting true multiplexing of rare bright QSOs needed for high-S/N absorption-line studies. We present several wide-field patrol architectures capable of accessing the full HWO focal plane, including all-reflective and catadioptric relays, UV-transmitting fiber approaches, and advanced microshutter configurations. These concepts route light from ~20–25 targets into a single high-resolution UV spectrograph or a distributed array of compact mini-spectrographs. We assess optical performance, mechanical complexity, and interface requirements, and outline a practical development path with ground-based on-sky demonstrations.

Items.Authors: Woong-Seob Jeong, Youngsoo Jo, Yujin Yang, Myung Sang Huh, Gil Jae Lee, Jeonghyun Pyo
Items.Title: Fabrication and evaluation of aluminum image slicers for high-throughput IFU spectrograph
Items.Abstract: We present the development and of aluminum image slicers intended for use in astronomical spectrographs. The image slicer is fabricated from aluminum materials using a diamond-turning machine equipped with customized end mills. Machining parameters were optimized through test cuts on aluminum materials, establishing stable mirror-finish conditions with an average surface roughness of ~10 nm. After optimization for prototype slicers, we achieved average surface roughness values of 10-13 nm, demonstrating reproducible smooth surfaces over the full array of slicer facets. These results confirm that direct diamond-turning machining of RSA6061 can meet the surface quality required for high-throughput, low-scatter reflective image slicers. We outline the planned integration of the fabricated image slicer into a prototype Integral-Field-Unit (IFU) spectrograph and discuss the expected improvement in observing efficiency for future ground-based and space-based instruments.

Items.Authors: Ceiwynn C. Longworth, Megan M. Delamer, Suvrath Mahadevan, Joe P. Ninan, Kathleen Gehoski
Items.Title: Fabrication of focusing optics for TA-MOONS
Items.Abstract: Tackling open problems in star formation requires precise spectroscopic observations of a large number of young stellar objects, spanning a wide wavelength band from the optical through the near-infrared. The TIFR-ARIES Multi-Object Optical to Near-infrared Spectrometer (TA-MOONS) is a new astronomical instrument designed to survey young stars. To precisely position starlight into its 8 robotic arms, an array of microscopic, concave mirrors is needed. The fabrication of the mirror array called Micro-MOONS was done using two-photon polymerization 3D printing. The mirrors are created of IP-S photoresist on a silicon substrate, with fabrication focusing on uniformity, minimizing surface roughness, and preserving the desired curvature radius.

Items.Authors: Cecilia R. Fasano, Chi C. Cheung, Marc Christophersen
Items.Title: Fabrication of near-UV multilevel diffractive lenses using grayscale e-beam lithography and TASTE
Items.Abstract: Advancements in the technologies used to observe the Ultraviolet (UV) bandpass (900-4000 Å) are necessary to enable the next generation of UV observatories. Optical components, including gratings and lenses, used in UV instruments can be improved via advanced techniques developed for the semiconductor fabrication industry. In particular, the evolution of grayscale lithography enables the creation of more complex 3D structures at micron- to nanometer-length scales. We report on efforts to use grayscale electron beam lithography (EBL) in combination with thermally activated selective topography equilibration (TASTE) to fabricate multilevel diffractive lenses (MDLs) in poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) for use in the near-UV where PMMA exhibits high transmission.     This work was supported by the Office of Naval Research.   Distribution Statement A. Approved for public release; distribution is unlimited.

Items.Authors: Philipp Huke, Viljon Sekseni, Kersten Mumme, Freerk Schütt, Dhruti Mavani, Lakshay Rajput, Imke Ottersberg, Miriam Brandt
Items.Title: Fast-controlled fiber-telescope interface for astrophysics
Items.Abstract: Small-scale telescopes connected with fibers allow the use of small-scale high-resolution spectrographs. This is interesting for telescopes with diameter even below one meter. Combining multiple telescopes is even more interesting as it allows to get a large amount of photons at a low cost. The CREOL-group demonstrated the capacity of a fiber-connected multi-telescope approach. Fiber-connected telescopes require demanding accurate alignment of the starlight in the focal plane. While at large telescope the tip-tilt control suffices smaller telescopes have to be adjusted themselves.  We present here a solution based on a fast control loop (up to 100Hz) that allows the accurate positioning of the fiber in the focal plane. A fiber-bundle with 19 fibers is used with the central fiber feeding the spectrograph. Light from the targeted star that enters the surrounding control-fibers is detected. The fast positioning is realized by a piezostage while for slow movements the telescope is adjusted

Items.Authors: Alexia Landry, E J Zinat Sathi, Julia Bryant, Heike Ebendorff-Heidepriem, Yunle Wei
Items.Title: First hexabundle optical fibre imaging bundles for the infrared
Items.Abstract: After the success of optical fibre imaging bundles “hexabundles”, for IFS on telescopes such as the Anglo-Australian telescope, there is a desire for hexabundles that work in the near-infrared for use on large wide-field telescopes. New hexabundles being developed at Astralis-USyd are the first fibre bundles for astronomy in the near-infrared with optical performance suitable for next generation telescopes. Until recent developments, hexabundles made of infrared optical fibre, ZBLAN, would have been impossible due to the performance and fragile nature of the material. However substantial improvements to the ZBLAN preform at Adelaide University have enabled a more robust fibre that now makes infrared hexabundles viable. We will present the optical and FRD performance of the newly improved ZBLAN fibres and initial infrared hexabundles.

Items.Authors: Zhengqi Sun
Items.Title: Flatness optimization strategy for cryogenic MOSAIC focal plane arrays: a finite element analysis and shim-based compensation method
Items.Abstract: This paper proposes a flatness optimization method for a cryogenic 4×4 GSENSE1517BSI sCMOS mosaic array. Addressing the challenge of thermo-mechanical deformation in SiC-packaged sensors mounted on Invar backplates, we utilize Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to predict surface warping caused by cooling to -40°C and gravity loads. We introduce a quantitative compensation algorithm that leverages the sensor's 3-point mounting interface to calculate optimal shim thicknesses for room-temperature assembly. The results demonstrate that this predictive compensation strategy effectively neutralizes thermal shrinkage and manufacturing tolerances, ensuring superior co-planarity for high-precision scientific imaging.

Items.Authors: Edoardo Alaimo, Fabio D'Anca, Daniele Spiga, Ugo Lo Cicero, Michela Todaro, Luisa Sciortino, Federico Fiorentino, Fabio Reale, Gabriele Cozzo, Pekka T. Törmä, Bahawal Haq, Daniele Brienza, Denise Perrone, Marco Stangalini, Marco Barbera
Items.Title: Flight-oriented design reconfiguration and diffractive effects analysis of CNT-based entrance filters for the MUSE EUV spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The NASA MUSE mission is developed to target key astrophysical questions about the solar corona with its first-ever high-resolution, both in time and in angle, EUV spectroscopy images; thus, diffraction impacts due to the entrance optical blocking filters (OBFs) must be thoroughly studied. We present flight-oriented updates to the MUSE entrance CNT-based OBFs proposed after the results of mechanical vibration tests performed on Structural/Thermal-Model filters. While they resisted qualification loads, higher-stress tests showed partial failure due to excessive dynamic differential pressure. A metal honeycomb supporting structure replacing the finer CNT-based mesh, and a thicker CNT-membrane used to increase, robustness are employed. Initial simulations indicate negligible diffraction relative to the PSF core at detector resolution, and also reduced intensity of secondary-order lobes compared to earlier designs. Updated core-PSF throughput estimates are compared to heritage solutions.

Items.Authors: Maxime Rombach, Jean-David Perriard, Laurent Chevalley, Jean-Paul Kneib
Items.Title: Focal plate prototyping for modular focal planes of stage-5 instruments for ground-based telescopes
Items.Abstract: Focal plate structures for Stage-5 instruments are a central part of the focus and tolerance chain of the optical fibers positionning. Prototyping such structures is therefore critical in the development of the next generation of highly multiplexed instruments.  This paper presents the manufacturing and measurements processes of a prototype of such a plate. A first assembly, integration and verification of the fiber positioner modules will also be proposed.

Items.Authors: Tyrone Woods, Patrick Côté, John S. Pazder, Matthew A. Taylor
Items.Title: FORECASTOR: getting ready for the next generation flagship UV space telescope
Items.Abstract: The Cosmological Advanced Survey Telescope for Optical and ultraviolet Research (CASTOR) will provide an essential bridge in the post-Hubble era, preventing a protracted UV-optical gap in space astronomy, and enabling an enormous range of discovery opportunities from the solar system to the nature of the Cosmos. FORECASTOR (Finding Optics Requirements and Exposure times for CASTOR) will supply a coordinated suite of mission-planning tools that will serve as the one-stop shop for proposal preparation, data reduction, and analysis for the CASTOR mission in an open-source and user-friendly format. In this talk, I'll present the latest results of this effort, including photometric and spectroscopic exposure time calculators, image simulation tools for galactic and resolved stellar populations, and survey scheduling tools, and provide illustrative science cases illustrating their use and the unprecedented capabilities of the CASTOR mission.

Items.Authors: Zou Xusheng, Guifeng Chen, Yonggang Gu, Chao Zhai
Items.Title: FPGA-accelerated fiber optic position detection
Items.Abstract: The current LAMOST（Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope）system employs high-resolution cameras with numerous fibers requiring detection and positioning. However, the host computer's processing speed is inadequate, causing each fiber image analysis to take over ten seconds, which significantly hinders rapid fiber positioning and control. To address the need for rapid and precise positioning of massive fiber spots in high-resolution images, this paper proposes a FPGA-based parallelized algorithm for spot center extraction. A new run-length encoding recognition algorithm for connected domain design is developed, incorporating label removal and equivalence table mechanisms to significantly reduce resource consumption. Through a parallel pipeline processing architecture, the system achieves high-speed image acquisition and sub-pixel-level spot center localization.

Items.Authors: Aurelie Magniez, Peter Wizinowich, Robert J. Harris, Tim Morris, Emily Ronson
Items.Title: From glass to print: 3D printed pyramids as wavefront sensors
Items.Abstract: Pyramid wavefront sensors (PWFS) are central to the next generation of high-contrast astronomical adaptive optics (AO) systems thanks to their high sensitivity. Current challenges associated with the manufacture of 4-facet glass pyramids or pairs of roof prisms include the difficulty and cost of achieving the requirements on flatness, edge-sharpness and achromaticity. These constraints limit design flexibility and restrict deployment of high-performance PWFS in current and future instruments.    High-precision 3D optical printing offers a promising alternative. Polymer-based additive fabrication enables compact, low-cost components with sub-micron surface accuracy, custom apex geometries, and thicknesses far smaller than achievable in glass. This work presents the first fabrication, testing on the POPY bench and analysis of 3D-printed pyramids for PWFS, including inverted designs and integrated spatial-filtering features impossible to realize using conventional optics.

Items.Authors: Markus Feldt, Thomas Bertram, Falk Eilenberger, Camille Graf, Pascal Jaufmann, Maud Langlois, Andreas Obereder, Raphael Pourcelot, Silvia Scheithauer, Horst Steuer
Items.Title: From METIS towards PCS: sequential closed-loop operation of a hybrid pyramid-Zernike sensor for extreme AO at the ELT
Items.Abstract: Both the Zernike and the pyramid wavefront sensor belong to the class of Fourier filtering sensors. Yet they vary greatly in terms of dynamic range, linearity, and sensitivity. The classical solution when both is needed is to operate these two (or similar) sensors in a dual-stage system, where the Zernike sensor would be located downstream of the pyramid.    A more cost-effective approach would be to devise a hybrid concept that can operate as one or the other, in temporally sequential order. So-called meta materials enable the creation of focal-plane phase masks for Fourier filtering sensors, which were only possible in computer simulations until recently.     We will present simulation results regarding the switch-over phase between the two concepts, and regarding the challenges resulting from controlling a single, high-precision, low dynamic range sensor in dual-stage closed loop. In addition, we will show initial ideas for realizing a corresponding phase plate.

Items.Authors: Janina Krieg, Clemens Kunisch, Thorsten Gehindy, Ralf Jedamzik, Thomas Westerhoff
Items.Title: Fused, closed-back ZERODUR® mirror substrates: meeting the stringent requirements of ELT M5-like mirrors
Items.Abstract: ZERODUR® glass-ceramic is renowned for its near-zero thermal expansion, making it a leading choice for high-precision mirror substrates in astronomy and space missions. SCHOTT’s innovative adhesive-free fusing technology for closed-back, lightweight ZERODUR® mirrors aims to meet stringent requirements for weight, stiffness, and thermal stability, such as for ESO’s ELT M5-like mirrors. This work presents FEM analysis results demonstrating the potential of these fused substrates to deliver the needed performance in advanced optical applications.

Items.Authors: Nate S. Osikowicz, Christine E. Gregg, Kenneth C. Cheung, Puneet Singla
Items.Title: Geometric analysis and prestress characterization of a modular multi-aperture RF reflector
Items.Abstract: This paper assesses the feasibility of a robotically assembled multi-aperture reflector exceeding 100 meters in diameter. As of yet, spaceborne reflectors have not been deployed at this scale due to the limited volume constraints of modern launch vehicles. However, in-space assembly could cross this threshold and enable greater observational capabilities in space. To this end, a robotic structural system is presented that makes use of cable actuated prism modules as building blocks for a reflective surface. The system can be assembled in a planar configuration and then reconfigured into any spherical surface by varying the ratio of top and bottom faces (the skew ratio) via cable actuation. The range of radius of curvature and reflector diameter are dictated by the prism’s skew ratio and height, respectively, yielding greater mission adaptivity than traditional ring truss designs without sacrificing structural stiffness.

Items.Authors: Jessica R. Zheng, Andrew Rakich, Christopher Coote, Jonathan S. Lawrence
Items.Title: GNAO AOB: optical design and key performance
Items.Abstract: The Gemini North Adaptive Optics Bench (GNAO AOB) is the next-generation adaptive optics facility for the Gemini North telescope, to be deployed at the Cassegrain focal plane. Designed to support wide-field surveys and time-domain science in the era of JWST and Rubin Observatory operations, GNAO AOB provides a substantial upgrade in AO performance, reliability, and operational flexibility over the current facility. Following a successful Preliminary Design Review, the baseline optical configuration has been finalized. This paper presents the final optical design and associated performance metrics. It demonstrates that the design meets all system-level requirements.

Items.Authors: Gaetano Sivo, Celia Blain, Masen Lamb, Martin Tschimmel, Andreas Seifahrt, Tim Gaggstatter, Joseph D'Amato, Julia Scharwächter, Shawn Barbod, Molly Grogan, Ricardo Cardenes, Jed Diller, Pedro Gigoux, Heather Carr, Logan Sato, Thomas Schneider, Brian Chinn, Christine Ricardo, Christophe Clergeon, Stan Karewicz, Elka Koehler, Ruben Diaz, Vincent Garrel, Thomas Hayward, Elena Sabbi, Stephen Goodsell, Scott Dahm, Andrew Adamson, Emanuele Piersanti, Marco Girardini, Giulia Tollero, Jonathon S. Lawrence, Yizheng Wang, Michael Goodwin, Benoît Neichel, Thierry Fusco, Julien Charton, Carlos Correia, Pierre Jouve, Sylvain Cetre, Andrew Rakich, Jessica Zheng, Christopher Coote, Summer Luo, Tomothy Chin, Zhemin Cai, Ali Ghari Zadeh, Dani Guzman, Helen McGregor, Anne-Sophie Bruni-Favier, Delphine Barbon-Dubosc, Tony J. Farrell, Lewis Waller, Julie Magri, Daniel Kerley, Edward L. Chapin, Jean-Pierre Veran, Suresh Sivanandam, Uriel Conod, Adam Muzzin, Nelson Nunes
Items.Title: GNAO: the new AO facility for Gemini North: beginning the AIV phase
Items.Abstract: The next-generation Gemini North Adaptive Optics (GNAO) project will position the Gemini North telescope as a premier high-spatial-resolution facility for survey science and transient follow-up in the rapidly evolving landscape of astronomical facilities. GNAO will use four laser guide stars to provide the Gemini North telescope with a state-of-the-art wide-field AO facility for observations at near-infrared wavelengths. GNAO is designed to be fully integrated into the Gemini queue scheduling. The f/32 output beam of GNAO is optimized to feed GIRMOS (Gemini Infrared Multi-Object Spectrograph) offering multiplexed integral field unit (IFU) spectroscopy with powerful survey capabilities compared to existing single-IFU instruments. In this presentation we report on the progress made during this last design phase and provide updates on our Final Design path forward including details on the AO Bench design, the RTC, the LGS Facility and the Control SW.

Items.Authors: Hu Zou
Items.Title: GOTTA prototype telescope: data reduction and preliminary results from the pilot survey
Items.Abstract: The Global Open Transient Telescope Array (GOTTA) is an ambitious project to build a network of wide-field telescopes. Its goal is to survey the entire optical sky with a 30-minute cadence to a depth of ~21.5 mag. This capability will revolutionize the study of transients by catching rare fast-evolving events and generating high-accuracy light curves. Over the past few years, we have developed a prototype telescope and conducted a six-month pilot survey. This talk introduces the prototype’s design, installation, operation, and our data reduction pipeline, and presents some early results. The prototype paves the way for the construction of the full GOTTA array.

Items.Authors: Ann Fitzpatrick, Joseph Mann, Joe Shreeves, Louis Saraff, Vonnie Von Cheng Lau, Carl Geddert, Emma Johnson, Martin Caldwell, Demet Ulusen Aksoy, Tom Wadsworth, Matthew Tildesley, Edgar Castillo-Domínguez, Eduard Muslimov, James Kariuki, Kieran McCall, Liam Boland
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: cryogenic lens mount prototyping – conclusions for the ICAM subsystem
Items.Abstract: The previous baseline design for HARMONI had four near-IR cameras each with 5 lenses. We present the AIT prototyping work and metrology used to characterise the alignment of a representative lens in a mount ring using previously trialled assembly procedure. The achieved alignment is characterised and compared to previous results. Changes to tilt and centration of the optical axis relative to the mount ring in operational conditions (130 K) are discussed and a study to compare the alignment changes due to the effects of temperature and gravity is also presented.

Items.Authors: Johan D. Floriot, Jean-François Sauvage, Zalpha Challita, Quentin Royer, Mélissa Alliguié, Kjetil Dohlen, Bastien Aqua, William Bon, David Le Mignant, Anne Costille
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: Prototype developments for the SCAOS object-selection and dichroic exchange modules
Items.Abstract: The HARMONI SCAO (Single-Conjugate Adaptive Optics) operational is enabled by the SCAOS subsystem which consists of a deployable dichroic beam splitter (SDM) and an optical bench including object selection (SOSM), beam control opto-mechanics and the pyramid wavefront sensor.   The SOSM allows the two-dimensional navigation within the 20 arcseconds diameter patrol field of the SCAOS and then to select an off-axis objects.  The SDM is a translation stage that permits to precisely and repeatably position each dichroic plate in the HARMONI optical beam allowing it to reflect blue light to the SCAOS modules while transmitting the red light of the beam to the science spectrograph system.   The current paper presents the qualification characterization performed on prototypes for the SCAOS object selection module (SOSM) and for the dichroic exchange module (SDM).

Items.Authors: Lazar G. Staykov, Tim J. Morris, Deborah Malone, Nazim Bharmal
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: pupil motion tracking and compensation using a wave-front sensor
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a software-based method for the real-time detection and compensation of the pupil motion. By analysing the intensity flux distribution across the wave-front sensor (WFS) sub-apertures, we compute the instantaneous pupil position and distribution and then, if motion is detected, dynamically update the system’s interaction matrix to account for any misalignment in real-time. We examine the performance of this algorithm in various operational conditions, including photon flux, WFS resolution, and wave-front shape and amplitude. Then we compare the results with existing pupil motion compensation techniques and finally discuss the applicability of this algorithm to the HARMONI at the ELT.

Items.Authors: Anne-Laure L. Cheffot, Amita Shrestha, Johannes Prell, Alexandru Duliu
Items.Title: Harnessing astronomy knowledge of telescopes to industrialise telescope production
Items.Abstract: In recent years, several publications have suggested that technologies and infrastructure developed for quantum communication could be leveraged to enable long-baseline interferometry. In this article, we provide an overview of the proposed technologies, their current capabilities, and the infrastructure being deployed across Europe. We examine how long-baseline infrared interferometry can benefit from these systems and which adaptations would be necessary to meet its specific requirements.

Items.Authors: Sébastien B. Vievard, Christopher Hamner, Nour Skaf, Michael Bottom, Mark Chun, Christoph Baranec, Olivier Guyon, Ellen Lee, Dylan Hively, Julien Lozi, Branden Allen, Guillermo Martin, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Manon Lallement, Vincent Déo
Items.Title: He'e-Lab: a modular testbed for astrophotonics and wavefront sensing development
Items.Abstract: Advanced astronomical instrumentation requires accessible platforms to test novel technologies and algorithms. We present the Hawaii Experimental Engineering Lab (He'e-Lab), a modular testbed for wavefront sensing and astrophotonics development. The lab supports: (A) integration and characterization of photonics components in real-time computing environments prior to telescope deployment, and (B) development of wavefront sensing and control algorithms. The testbed features a supercontinuum source (500 nm - 2 μm), a 1k-actuator Boston Micromachines deformable mirror, and downstream instrumentation including photonics injection with a mid-resolution (R~3,000) spectrograph for visible (600-800 nm) wavelengths. Wavefront sensing capabilities include a HASO 126 Shack-Hartmann sensor with planned expansion to emerging technologies. A 37-segment mirror with piston-tip-tilt control enables cophasing research. This platform supports collaborative research, technology development, and education.

Items.Authors: Aaron Omadutt, Roelof S. de Jong, Joe Barrow, Jon Lawrence
Items.Title: High multiplex and precision: the design and development of FLEX, a grid-based fibre positioner with large patrol radius and minimized telecentric error
Items.Abstract: The Fibre Location EXtender (FLEX) is a novel fibre positioner designed to operate within highly constrained focal surfaces in next-generation spectroscopic facilities, such as the Wide-Field Spectroscopic Telescope (which requires 32,000 fibres in a 1.4 m diameter focal surface).  FLEX aims to surpass current available positioner metrics by substantially increasing the fibre patrol radius while minimizing both telecentric error and space between positioners for high multiplex. The patented design uses nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy) in three concentric tubes, maintaining the fibre tip's parallel orientation during tilting. The 110mm-long assembly achieves dense packing with a minimum achievable pitch of ≈5.9mm and a large patrol radius of ≈17mm with a telecentric error of 0.3 degrees when fully extended. Coupled with three piezoelectric actuators, FLEX provides tip, tilt, and piston motion for a large coverage area and vertical refocusing. Initial prototyping results will be presented.

Items.Authors: Maria Vincent, Charlotte E. Guthery, Scott Lilley, Michael Bottom, Sylvain Cetre, Luke Gers, Sonia Karkar, Eduardo Marin, Johnny Tam, Jonathan Steiner, Jacob Taylor, Tatum Umiamaka, Ed Wetherell, Peter Wizinowich, Antonin Bouchez
Items.Title: High order advanced Keck adaptive optics: results from lab integration and testing of the high order deformable mirror
Items.Abstract: The High Order Advanced Keck Adaptive Optics (HAKA) upgrade will lower residual wavefront error on the Keck II telescope, and enable detailed characterization of older exoplanets, protoplanetary disks, and stars near the Galactic Center. HAKA replaces the original 349-actuator Xinetics deformable mirror with a 2,844-actuator ALPAO magnetic voice-coil DM, upgrades the Shack–Hartmann wavefront sensor, and implements advanced wavefront-control algorithms. The new DM arrived in summer 2025, underwent site-acceptance testing, and some additional tests while integrated with the lab test bench from July 2025 to January 2026. We present the acceptance-test bench design and alignment, closed-loop WFS configuration, and a modular Python control/analysis framework linking the ALPAO SDK to a Zygo interferometer via RPC and interfacing to the real-time controller. Final lab results include DM performance metrics and closed-loop stability demonstrating summit installation readiness.
